title: Episode 277: John Glenn: Friendship 7, Three Orbits Around the Earth, and the Return at Seventy-Seven
description:
The iconic, patriotic, and enduring life of John Herschel Glenn Jr.: the Marine fighter ace, Mercury Seven astronaut, and long-serving United States Senator who became the first American to orbit the Earth. Flying one hundred and forty-nine combat missions in World War Two and Korea, Glenn set a transcontinental supersonic speed record before being chosen among America's original seven astronauts. On February 20, 1962, strapped atop a temperamental Atlas rocket aboard 'Friendship 7', Glenn orbited the Earth three times, enduring a malfunctioning control system and a terrifying reentry when his heat shield was feared to be loose. Thirty-six years later, at the age of seventy-seven, Glenn returned to space aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery, proving that human potential has no age limit. Discover an American legend.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans series celebrates the pioneering astronaut and public servant whose historic orbital flight galvanized a nation in the race to the stars. Here is George with the extraordinary life of John Glenn.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE PRIDE OF NEW CONCORD: 1921 TO 1941
Born in July 1921 in Cambridge, Ohio, and raised in the close-knit village of New Concord, John Herschel Glenn Jr. embodied the small-town Midwestern virtues of faith, discipline, and patriotism. His father John Sr. ran a plumbing business and Chevrolet dealership; his mother Clara was an elementary school teacher. From early childhood, John shared an unbreakable bond with his childhood sweetheart Anna Margaret Castor—Annie—whom he met in a playpen at age two and married in 1943. An accomplished high school athlete and scholar, Glenn earned his private pilot's license in 1941 while studying chemistry at Muskingum College. When Imperial Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, Glenn immediately volunteered for naval aviation cadet training, entering the United States Marine Corps as a second lieutenant and discovering his true vocation in the cockpits of military combat aircraft.  Growing up in New Concord during the depths of the Great Depression, John learned the sacred obligations of civic duty and community mutual aid, watching his father extend credit to impoverished farmers who could not pay for plumbing repairs. His boyhood courtship of Annie Castor was a heartwarming lifelong romance: Annie suffered from a severe, debilitating stutter that rendered her eighty-five percent speech impaired, and John became her devoted protector, never allowing anyone to tease her and patiently listening to her every word. When John enlisted in the Marines following the attack on Pearl Harbor, he promised Annie that no matter where the storms of war carried him, his heart would always remain anchored to her in Ohio.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: 'MAGNET ASS' AND PROJECT BULLET: WORLD WAR TWO, KOREA, AND SUPERSONIC SPEED: 1944 TO 1957
During World War Two, Glenn flew fifty-nine combat missions in the Pacific theater, piloting F4U Corsair fighter-bombers over the Marshall Islands. When the Korean War erupted, Glenn flew an additional ninety combat missions, dodging heavy anti-aircraft fire and earning the admiring nickname 'Magnet Ass' from fellow pilots after bringing his Corsair and F9F Panther jets home riddled with over two hundred and fifty flak holes. Flying alongside baseball legend Ted Williams as his wingman, Glenn shot down three Soviet MiG-15s over the Yalu River in the final weeks of the war. Becoming a military test pilot at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, Maryland, Glenn made aviation history on July 16, 1957, in 'Project Bullet'. Flying a Vought F8U-1P Crusader from Los Angeles to New York, Glenn completed the first continuous transcontinental supersonic flight in three hours, twenty-three minutes, and eight seconds, averaging supersonic velocity and becoming a national celebrity.  During intense dive-bombing runs over the Marshall Islands and Korean valleys, Glenn became legendary for pressing his bombing attacks to dangerously low altitudes to ensure pinpoint accuracy against fortified enemy positions. When his Corsair was hit by heavy 37-millimeter anti-aircraft shells that blew massive holes through his fuselage and tail surfaces, Glenn calmly feathered his propeller, stabilized his flight trim, and brought his shredded fighter safely back to base, demonstrating an instinctive aerodynamic feel for damaged aircraft. His historic 1957 transcontinental flight in Project Bullet was an engineering masterpiece, requiring three aerial refuelings over Texas and Kansas from propeller-driven tankers while flying at supersonic cruising speeds.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE MERCURY SEVEN AND THE BATTLE OF THE ASTRONAUTS: 1959 TO 1961
In April 1959, NASA introduced the 'Mercury Seven'—the seven military test pilots selected from hundreds of elite applicants to pioneer human spaceflight. Among flamboyant comrades, Glenn stood out for his clean-cut demeanor, devoted Presbyterian faith, and eloquent defense of traditional American values during press conferences. Behind the scenes, Glenn was fiercely competitive, pushing himself through grueling centrifuge rides, heat chambers, and isolation tests. When Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space in April 1961, followed by Alan Shepard and Gus Grissom's fifteen-minute suborbital hops, the pressure on NASA to achieve full orbital flight was immense. NASA selected Glenn to fly the first crewed orbital mission, assigning him the spacecraft he christened 'Friendship 7'.  In the fiercely competitive pressure cooker of the Mercury space program, Glenn stood out as the natural leader and moral compass of the original astronaut corps, waking at dawn for solitary five-mile runs along the Florida beaches while other pilots frequented Cocoa Beach nightspots. When Life magazine purchased exclusive rights to the astronauts' personal stories, Glenn insisted that their public image reflect dignity, humility, and family devotion, articulating the deep spiritual faith that sustained him through perilous centrifuge runs and survival training. When Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev bragged that Soviet cosmonaut Gherman Titov had completed seventeen orbits around the Earth, President John F. Kennedy turned to Glenn to restore America's prestige on the global stage.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: FRIENDSHIP 7: 'GODSPEED, JOHN GLENN': FEBRUARY 20, 1962
On the morning of February 20, 1962, after ten agonizing weather delays, forty-year-old John Glenn was strapped into Friendship 7 atop an Atlas D rocket at Launch Complex 14 at Cape Canaveral. At nine forty-seven in the morning, as the Atlas rocket ignited and lifted from the pad, backup astronaut Scott Carpenter radioed from the blockhouse the immortal blessing: 'Godspeed, John Glenn.' Reaching orbit at seventeen thousand five hundred miles per hour, Glenn looked out his small periscope and rectangular window, marveling at the radiant blue arc of the Earth below: 'That view is tremendous,' he reported. Over Australia, the citizens of Perth turned on all their municipal streetlights and porch lamps in middle-of-the-night solidarity, creating a glowing beacon visible from space. Orbiting the globe once every eighty-eight minutes, Glenn observed mysterious luminous 'fireflies' swirling around his capsule at orbital sunrise, later identified as tiny ice crystals venting from the spacecraft's heat exchanger.  Staring out the small viewing window of Friendship 7 as he soared over the Indian Ocean at five miles a second, Glenn experienced a mystical awe at the breathtaking tapestry of the globe: sunsets were dazzling displays of blinding orange, electric blue, and deep violet that wrapped around the planet in seconds. As Friendship 7 crossed the western coast of Australia in the pitch black of night, the city of Perth glowed like a diamond in the desert, a magnificent gesture of human solidarity that moved Glenn to radio his heartfelt gratitude to the people below. The mysterious swirling 'fireflies' that accompanied his spacecraft at orbital sunrise baffled NASA flight directors, creating a poetic, enchanting mystery that captured the imagination of the entire world.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE FLAMING REENTRY AND THE LOOSE HEAT SHIELD: FEBRUARY 20, 1962
During Glenn's second orbit, mission controllers in Mercury Control detected an alarming telemetry signal: Segment 51 indicated that the capsule's primary landing bag and ablative heat shield were no longer locked in place. If the heat shield detached during atmospheric reentry, Friendship 7 would be vaporized in seconds by three-thousand-degree frictional plasma. Flight Director Chris Kraft made the unprecedented decision to order Glenn not to jettison his retro-rocket pack after retro-fire, hoping the metal straps would hold the heat shield against the capsule during reentry. Entering the upper atmosphere over the Pacific, Glenn endured severe G-forces as the retro-pack broke apart in flaming orange debris, hurtling past his window. A terrifying four-minute radio blackout enveloped the capsule. In mission control and across millions of television sets, the nation held its breath in silence until Glenn's calm, steady voice crackled through the static: 'Boy, that was a real fireball of a ride... my condition is good.' Friendship 7 splashed down safely in the Atlantic Ocean near Grand Turk Island.  The four-minute radio blackout during Friendship 7's fiery atmospheric reentry was an agonizing crucible of suspense for millions of Americans glued to their television screens, listening to Walter Cronkite's solemn broadcasts. Inside the tiny capsule, temperatures soared as frictional atmospheric compression generated a glowing wall of superheated plasma that engulfed the exterior in roaring orange flames. Large, burning chunks of the strapped retro-rocket pack sheared past Glenn's window, slamming against the hull as the capsule decelerated violently under eight Gs of gravitational force. Glenn remained remarkably calm, maintaining manual fly-by-wire attitude control until his drogue parachute deployed with a reassuring jolt over the choppy Atlantic waves.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SENATE STATESMAN AND ANNIE'S CHAMPION: 1964 TO 1997
Paraded before four million cheering spectators in New York City's ticker-tape parade, President John F. Kennedy privately decided that Glenn was too valuable a national symbol to risk in further spaceflights. Entering politics, Glenn was elected to the United States Senate from Ohio in 1974, serving twenty-four distinguished years. A master of legislative detail, Glenn became chairman of the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, authoring the landmark Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act of 1978 and fighting for veterans' benefits and scientific research. Throughout his public life, Glenn remained fiercely devoted to his wife Annie, who overcame a severe childhood stutter at age fifty-three to become a national advocate for people with speech disorders. Glenn's integrity and bipartisan decency earned him the respect of colleagues across the political spectrum.  Throughout his distinguished twenty-four years in the United States Senate, Glenn was renowned as a tireless workhorse rather than a political showhorse, mastering complex technical nuances of nuclear non-proliferation, governmental ethics, and civil service reform. Glenn was fiercely proud of his beloved wife Annie, who at age fifty-three underwent intensive speech therapy in Virginia to conquer her lifelong stutter, subsequently traveling the nation delivering inspiring public speeches to encourage children and adults with communication disorders. Glenn's unwavering integrity, Midwestern warmth, and deep patriotism made him an elder statesman of the republic, respected and revered by colleagues across the political divide.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE RETURN TO THE STARS AT SEVENTY-SEVEN: 1998 AND LEGACY
In January 1998, thirty-six years after orbiting the Earth in Friendship 7, NASA announced that seventy-seven-year-old Senator John Glenn would return to space as a payload specialist aboard the Space Shuttle Discovery on STS-95. Glenn underwent months of rigorous physical training, offering his own body as an experimental laboratory to study the biological parallels between the aging process and the physiological effects of microgravity on bone density, immune response, and sleep cycles. On October 29, 1998, Discovery blasted into orbit from Kennedy Space Center, carrying the oldest human being ever to fly in space. During nine days in orbit, Glenn conducted eighty-three scientific experiments, smiling as he gazed once more upon the radiant blue planet. Passing away in December 2016 at the age of ninety-five, John Glenn was laid to rest with full military honors at Arlington National Cemetery. From the trenches of the South Pacific to the outer reaches of the cosmos, John Glenn's life proved that courage, duty, and the spirit of discovery are eternal.  When seventy-seven-year-old Senator Glenn strapped into the mid-deck of Space Shuttle Discovery on STS-95 in October 1998, he carried with him the pride and admiration of an entire nation that had grown up alongside his heroic journey. Floating weightlessly through Discovery's flight deck, Glenn looked down at the radiant curve of the Earth with the same boyish wonder he had felt thirty-six years earlier aboard Friendship 7, marveling at how space travel had evolved from a solitary, cramped capsule into a spacious international laboratory. John Glenn's monumental life spanned the entire arc of modern aviation, from open-cockpit biplanes to supersonic fighters and reusable space shuttles, leaving behind an immortal legacy of courage, service, and unshakeable faith in the boundless potential of the human spirit.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. John Glenn's daring orbital journey, decades of honorable public service, and triumphant return to space at seventy-seven remain a shining chapter in the American story. Join us next week as Rebecca returns with Part Nine of our Top 50 Americans series, honoring the legendary sports and cultural icons who transformed American society. Until then, stay curious.
